Fitzgerald (1888) studied the pollination of Spiranthes australis in the vicinity of Sydney, the type location for the species, and concluded that the pollinia were so tightly encased in the anther that they could not be extracted and the flowers were self-pollinating - in his very unusual and descriptive wording ‘in my opinion it is never made fruitful by the pollen from another flower.’ However, the self-pollination process in these central N.S.W. plants is not straightforward because there is no obvious rostellum separating the anther and the stigma and the pollen grains do not simply fall onto the stigma or come into contact with its upper surface. It is quite possible these plants are apomictic. By contrast, plants from some areas have functional pollinia attached to a removable viscidium and are probably insect-pollinated; in others the viscidium is abortive meaning that the pollinarium cannot be extracted from the flowers as a unit. Flowers of this latter type can also have loosely packed, friable pollinia and are commonly either self-pollinating via the pollen falling onto the stigma, or apomictic. Insect-pollinated flowers of S. australis are often visited by small, dark, native bees which work their way upward on the spikes, probing deep into the flowers for nectar and during the process picking up pollinia on the face around the mouthparts. It has been reported in Vic. that the flowers of S. australis are pollinated by at least 2 species of small native bees (Halictus sp. and Coelioxys albolineata) that climb head first into the tubular labellum and emerge head first after turning around inside the flower (Coleman 1931, 1933). Photos of 3 species of native bee visiting Spiranthes flowers can be seen in Kuiter (2013, pp. 106--107, 2016, pp. 106--109).

Prolonged consumption by stock can cause chronic kidney damage and death (Conn et al. 1999). Salter (1944) noted that Oxalis pes-caprae is a variable species. Michael (1964), after studying many of the populations across southern Australia, concluded that ''considerable'' variation existed within Australia, with differences in markings on the sepals, size and colouring of the petals, and differences in shape and markings on the leaflets. Peirce (1973, cited in Pierce 1997) identified additional variation in the leaflets illustrated by Michael (1964), from 6 to 13, in Western Australia. According to Michael (1964), the Australian populations are comprised predominantly of the short-styled pentaploid morph, and that as far as is known the pentaploid variant exists in only the short-styled morph. Michael (1964) also found that a mid-styled morph is also present in Australia. A number of flora accounts (e.g. Bennett 1987, Conn 1992, Conn et al. 1997) note that fruit was either not seen or not known in Australia. However, Michael (1964) found that in situations where different style-length forms are present, seed is freely produced. Jaspars (1986) notes that: "2 chromosome races occur here. The largest populations are the short-styled sterile pentaploids (5n = 35); there are also small populations of fertile tetraploids (4n = 28) with all 3 style-lengths."

Bird dispersed seeds. Extract from an article by Sara Freeland highlighting the importance of this plant to the Green Parrot's ecosystem on Norfolk Island: "An intriguing behaviour has been observed in Norfolk Island's Green Parrots (Cyanoramphus cookii). Birds have been spotted using native pepper trees (Piper excelsum) to help fend off pests and parasites. Green parrots were photographed and filmed biting off pieces of pepper tree shoots and bark, chewing them, and then rubbing the chewed material through their feathers. They also stripped leaves and rubbed their beaks along the branches before applying preen oil over themselves. Pepper Trees are known for their potent aromatic compounds, particularly piperine, which has insect-repellent and antimicrobial properties. This behaviour of self-anointing with plant material appears to help the parrots repel blood-sucking insects and other ectoparasites. While birds are known to use various methods to combat parasites, such as preening, dust-bathing, and anting (where they use ants to help clean their feathers), the use of plant materials for anointing is quite rare. Historical records and recent observations show that this behaviour is not entirely new but has been noted infrequently across different bird species - including some parrots in New Zealand and Darwin’s finches."

In Australia, Pittosporum bicolor hybridises easily with P. undulatum when these species occur sympatrically, but P. bicolor is easily distinguished from P. undulatum by differences in leaf size, shape and indumentum, and fruit morphology. Hybrids are becoming more frequent between P. bicolor and P. undulatum as the latter continues its range expansion. Pittosporum bicolor has rather narrow elliptic leaves with a persistent indumentum on the undersurface, maroon-streaked yellow flowers and black fruits with red seeds. Hybrids between these two taxa tend to have bicolor foliage (although wider and often longer), undulatum flowers (complete with vestigial staminodes) and fruits with orange seeds.

Pittosporum undulatum has a vigorous rhizomatous root system which survives all but the most intense wild fires, and a habit of holding the large leaves of its coppice growth horizontal blocks light for other seeds to germinate. This ensures very rapid colonisation, particularly on disturbed sites (Gleadow 1982). For details on biology and ecology see Mullett (2009) and references therein.

In 1956, R.C. Cooper stated that Pittosporum undulatum was naturally occurring in marginal rainforest throughout the coastal ranges of southeastern Australia. Grows in wet sclerophyll to sheltered dry sclerophyll forests and scrubs.

Originally southeastern Australia, from McPherson range in Southern Queensland to Victorian Alps in south-eastern Victoria. Recent range expansion into western Victoria, and grown and naturalised in most temperate parts of the world including: the Azores, California, Hawaii and Pacific islands, Sri-Lanka, Asia, and Africa.

Declared a weed in Victoria. Restricting horticultural plantings to just male plants is not a solution as most of these plants also produce occasional fruits; all forms are self-compatible and plants range from dioecious to monoecious. Neither the recent morphological nor the DNA analyses are informative on the affinities of this species. Noticeably the two truly wide-ranging/weedy Pittosporum species in Australia (P. undulatum and P. ferrugineum) both display the full spectrum of sex strategies from unisexual flowers with staminode or pistillode tissue, to perfect and clearly viable bisexual flowers, often in the same inflorescence. Hybrids are becoming more frequent between Pittosporum bicolor and P. undulatum as the latter continues its range expansion. Pittosporum bicolor has rather narrow elliptic leaves with a persistent indumentum on the undersurface, maroon streaked yellow flowers and black fruits with red seeds. Hybrids between these two taxa tend to have bicolor foliage (although wider and often longer), undulatum flowers (complete with vestigial staminodes) and fruits with orange seeds. For an account of Pittosporum undulatum on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands, where introduced and escaped from cultivation, see Green (1994: 158).

Callitriche antarctica occurs as a terrestrial, marginal or less often aquatic plant to a depth of 2.5 m on bare peat, sand, gravel or rocks. Throughout much of its range it is strongly associated with wet areas which are enriched with dung from marine mammals such as seal wallows. It also occurs in pool complex vegetation subject to low intensity use by moulting seals as well as Wandering Albatross and petrel nests, and abandoned penguin colonies. It often occurs where areas that are kept wet by seepages around the base of Poa cookii, P. foliosa or P. flabellata grass tussocks are damaged by animals. It occurs in and on the margins of still or slow-flowing water of seepages, streams, lakes, ponds and pools. It will occur in wetlands associated with raised beaches and coastal rocks with species such as Plantago barbata or Ranunculus crassipes, in bog pools with Azorella selago, Colobanthus kerguelensis, Poa cookii and Pringlea antiscorbutica, wet Deschampsia antarctica swards and flushes, bogs characterised by Juncus scheuchzerioides and Rostkovia sp., on seepages over rocks with Poa litorosa, Bulbinella rossii and Polystichum vestitum, and on disturbed ground such as roadsides.

It is a serious winter annual weed in both lowland and upland crops in Japan, and a major rice weed in Nepal (to 1900 m altitude) and the Philippines, as well as infesting rice in China, Taiwan and Hungary, and vegetables and vineyards (Holm et al. 1997). As a competitive weed A. aequalis can reduce cereal yields. The presence of this grass in the Murrumbidgee-Murray irrigation area and Riverina could indicate a potential for further spread and weed issues. Alopecurus aequalis is also an environmental weed, having been recorded in damp or ponded areas in eucalypt woodlands and on saltbush plains in New South Wales (based on herbarium records) and mallee bioregions in Victoria (The State of Victoria Department of Sustainability and Environment 2009), as well as creeks in a boggy subalpine area in Kosciuszko National Park. It is able to grow in shallow aquatic habitats.

Grows in wet places, including swampy areas, bogs, shallow pools, poorly drained areas (e.g. ponded or depressed areas on plains in native woodlands and shrublands), along streams, creeks and irrigation channels; to high altitudes; often aquatic with partly submerged stems.

Introduced; occurs in southeastern South Australia, western to northeastern Victoria and in the Kosciuszko area possibly W to far southwestern New South Wales. Native to most of Europe, Asia and N America; also naturalised in New Zealand.

The presence and distribution of Alopecurus aequalis in New South Wales and possibly elsewhere in Australia requires further investigation. There are specimens from the Cooleman Plain in Kosciuszko National Park with awns to 2 mm long attached just below the middle of the lemma at c. ⅖ of the lemma length from the base (similar to what occurs in A. aequalis specimens from overseas examined by P.G.K.). There is another group of specimens, often previously determined as A. geniculatus, which also have inconspicuous lemma awns and these specimens are from the Yanco-Berrigan-Hay-Barham area of the South Western Plains and probably extend west to Wentworth in the South Far Western Plains, e.g. 7.7 km SE along Conargo-Deniliquin (Jerilderie) road from the Cobb Hwy, M.F. Porteners 9009011 & V. Logan (NSW). In these specimens the straight to slightly recurved or outswept awns are often shorter (to 1.5 (-2) mm long), attached in the upper half of the lemma near the apex (to c. 0.5 (-0.7) mm below the apex) and usually more conspicuously exceed the apex of the glumes (i.e. extend further), and the folded glumes are characteristically slightly sigmoid in shape (the different spikelet forms are illustrated in Kodela 2015: 145, fig. 2). This latter group of specimens possibly represent another taxon, but the specimens have not been able to be matched with any other species of Alopecurus from exotic specimens held at MEL and NSW or from following the revision of the genus by Doğan (1999). Alternatively, they may simply reflect variation in A. aequalis where the lemma awn can be inserted from c. midway to subapical. This variation also occurs in Victoria, where specimens with awns inserted higher on the lemma (as in most of the southwestern New South Wales specimens) mainly come from the northwest of the State, fide N.G. Walsh (pers. comm.); see also Kodela (2015) for further discussion. There is also the possibility for hybrids between A. aequalis and A. geniculatus (= A. ×haussknechtianus Asch. & Graebn.). Alopecurus aequalis possibly also occurs in Tasmania as several specimens labelled as A. geniculatus have barely exserted, straight awns, e.g. Brumbys Creek, R.C. Gunn 1459 (NSW); Queenstown, c. 1932, D. Martin (NSW). The biostatus of Alopecurus aequalis in Australia (where collection records go back to c. 1880) warrants further investigation (see Kodela 2015 and notes under genus). Alopecurus aequalis is non toxic.

Amphipogon caricinus is closely related to A. strictus, from which it differs primarily in having intravaginal shoots often developing successively to produce obliquely ascending rhizomes, and often also further shoots from sheaths above the basal one. Additional features include generally longer panicles and a lack of large setae on glumes. Vickery (1950) also used as a differentiating feature the cilia on lobes of the lemma and palea continuing to the tip in A. caricinus var. caricinus, but tending to end before the apex, leaving a short scabrous tip in A. strictus. I have found this feature to be unreliable. In the zone where the ranges of the two species approach each other or overlap (e.g. south-eastern S.A. and the W.A. wheatbelt E and ESE of Perth), identification can be difficult, with plants bearing A. caricinus rhizomes sometimes having setae on the glumes. Despite these occasional unresolved difficulties, the two species are considered distinct. They can sometimes be found growing together and are readily distinguishable in their overlap zones. A variant in the Geraldton-Northampton area of W.A. has the rhizome structure of this species although the rhizome and lower sheaths are exceptionally hairy, and the glumes resemble those of A. strictus. This variant, placed in A. caricinus var. caricinus in this treatment, requires further study. Thereare two varieties.

Planted as a sand stabiliser in N.T. and coastal N.S.W. and persistent in some of these areas. A pantropical weed, distributed throughout the Old World Tropics, probably originating in Africa, and introduced into America. Dactyloctenium aegyptium is a common introduced species on Christmas Is. and grows as a weed on Cocos (Keeling) Is. Most common in disturbed areas but also present in open Eucalyptus forest on a variety of soils, and on coastal dunes.

As well as its value as a sand stabiliser, D. aegyptium is considered useful as pasture in some areas, and persists under grazing, but is reported (from overseas) to be rich in cyanogenic glycosides and therefore a danger to stock at certain times. Previously described as an annual, D. aegyptium frequently assumes a perennial, stoloniferous habit in Australia, and has been confused with the perennial D. australe. However, D. aegyptium is distinguished by the much shorter anthers and shorter rachis prolongation, with usually a greater number of spikes and with the abaxial side of leaf blades usually hairy from the base. It differs from the Australian endemic D. radulans in having a globoid rather than plano-convex or ellipsoid caryopsis, spikes usually longer and free from each other except at the base, and a taller habit. The differences between D. aegyptium and D. giganteum are discussed under the latter taxon. Bentham (Fl. Austral. 7: 615, 1878) incorrectly cited Persoon as the original author of Eleusine aegyptiaca. Since Willdenow used the epithet aegyptiacum rather than aegyptium, some sources have considered D. aegyptium (L.) P.Beauv. (1812) or D. aegyptium (L.) K.Richt. (1890) to be the validly published name. However, Willdenow refers to Cynosurus aegyptius in Sp. Pl. 1: 416 (1797) (= Cynosurus aegyptius L., Sp. Pl. 1: 72, 1753), and the epithet aegyptiacum is therefore considered to be an orthographic error which may be automatically corrected with use.

Dried specimens of E. ramosus are most reliably distinguished from those of E. acicularis by the combination of completely glabrous foliage (except for occasional hairs behind the ligule) and the absence of an external ligule. In addition, E. ramosus tends to be taller, with fewer spikes, and the culms branching at several nodes is distinctive in more mature specimens. The two species may be more readily distinguished in the field, as the spikes of E. ramosus are reported to spread in a single plane while those of E. acicularis are arranged in several planes. The leaves of E. ramosus are borne along the whole culm length, but are mostly basal in E. acicularis, though this may be partly related to the height. Abruptly twisting mature leaves have been seen on specimens of E. acicularis but this condition is more common in E. ramosus. Intermediates between these two species sometimes occur in N.S.W.

The former is more common, but the latter is seen in the type specimen. Distinguishing features include the form of the panicles; granular lemma and palea; heavy-textured glumes with thickened, scabrous keel; usually two stamens; and spikelets with a median depression above the rachilla. It intergrades with both the E. brownii/E. benthamii complex and with E. sororia. Eragrostis elongata and E. sororia can both be distinguished from the former complex in their typical condition by the presence of only two stamens, the shape and size of their grains, and their compactly spiciform panicles. The callus is entirely bearded (not mostly glabrous), and the glumes are broadly ovate-elliptic, obtuse, mucronate and 11--13-nerved (usually ovate, acuminate, muticous and 5--7-nerved in E. obtusa). Lepturus stoddartii Fosberg was described as differing from L. repens by possessing pairs of opposite spikelets in the middle part of the rachis, rather than alternate spikelets for the whole length, with transverse rather than oblique disarticulation of the rachis, and a well-developed second floret, and in being restricted to islands of the Great Barrier Reef. However, specimens from other areas such as islands of the Timor Sea have relatively large second florets, some even bisexual, while lacking any paired spikelets. Transverse articulation of the rachis also has been seen in specimens lacking paired spikelets. Opposite pairing of spikelets has been seen on specimens from near Brisbane, but not on all spikes of the same plant, and not all paired spikelets possess welldeveloped second florets. The presence of these intermediate forms, and their distribution, suggest that L. repens and L. stoddartii are conspecific. The opposite pairing of spikelets in the middle or lower rachis was considered sufficiently distinctive to retain the latter taxon as a subspecies at the time of publication of Fl. Australia Volume 43, but, since then, Kew duplicates of some specimens thought to be L. repens subsp. stoddartii have been found to have alternate spikelets throughout. Sand binder. Morphologically this species is very variable. Throughout the majority of its range T. loliiformis is characterised by short dense inflorescences with overlapping spikelets, e.g. D.J.Nelson 2293. In the east of the country (on the tablelands around Atherton in north-eastern Qld and the tablelands from southern Qld through to Vic.) specimens grade to having longer, less dense inflorescences with spikelets that are slightly overlapping to distant, e.g. A.C.Beauglehole 30668. This eastern group appears to have affinities with T. spicatus (Nees) Ekman (M.Lazarides, pers. comm.) from southern U.S.A. and Central and South America. The syntypes of Tripogon loliiformis cover the range of variation described above including the gradation between groups. Further taxonomic work is required to ascertain if T. spicatus can be applied to the eastern Australian material. For the present all material has been treated as Tripogon loliiformis.

Both these extreme forms and intermediates often occur on the same rhizome. All frond forms may be fertile, although the small forms are more likely to be sterile. We are defining this variety, var. dielsii, primarily on the position of the hydathodes and secondarily, on the presence of thicker and often truncate emarginate or notched fronds. If the character of persistent 'silver' abaxial indument is given undue emphasis, it is possible to find matching specimens over most of the range of Pyrrosia confluens. A similar situation arises if truncate fronds are used as the major distinguishing character. Pyrrosia confluens responds to environmental stress by producing smaller more leathery often truncate fronds. By emphasising the marginal hydathode position, and taking into account the other characters mentioned above, var. dielsii is confined more or less to the Atherton Tableland, Queensland, and var. confluens occurs over the remainder of the range. Hydathodes are usually best observed in young fronds, but may be concealed under the stellate hairs at all stages of growth. A magnification of × 10--20 is sometimes required to detect them, particularly if the white deposit has fallen.

A mangrove contributing to the functioning and stability of estuarine and tidal river ecosystems, providing habitat, shelter and a source of food (for aquatic and terrestrial organisms), maintaining water quality (filter and trap sediments and pollutants), soil stability, foreshore protection. Mangroves in the intertidal zone play an important role between the land and the sea. As breeding grounds for many fish, prawns, crabs and other shellfish, mangrove wetlands help maintain aquatic ecosystems which in turn support fisheries. Aegiceras corniculatum often occurs in mixed stands with Avicennia marina but usually grows in shallower water and will extend further upstream and occur more inland than that species (Sainty & Jacobs 1981, Harden 1990). Germination in Aegiceras corniculatum is viviparous, the seed germinates within the fruit while it is on the plant. Then when the fruit drops off it can float in the tidal water until lodging in a suitable habitat. The nectar of Aegiceras corniculatum is very attractive to bees.
This species is tolerant of a wide range of tidal environments. It is found along the banks of tidal creeks and estuaries usually on the seaward side of the mangrove community.

Extends around the Australian coastline from the Burrup Peninsula, Western Australia, (20° 41´ S) to southern New South Wales and Lord Howe Island. It is also found along the coastlines of neighbouring countries extending as far W as India.
For accounts of Aegiceras corniculatum on Lord Howe Island see Hutton (1986: 131; 2002: 82) and (Green (1994: 150).

The helicoid division of the fronds of most forms of this species has been described as pedate (e.g. F.L.E. Diels in H.G.A. Engler & K.A.E. Prantl, Die Naturlichen Pflanzenfamilien 1(4): 286, 1899), dichotomously branched, with unequal basal dichotomy (R.E. Holttum, A Revised Flora of Malaya 2: 603--604, 1968) or pedately subdichotomous (C.R.W.K. van Alderewelt van Rosenburgh, Malayan Ferns 333, 1908). These descriptive terms do not adequately describe the method of division. The basis of the anadromous frond architecture is that each successive basiscopic basal division of the 2 lowermost primary pinnae is well developed, i.e. they are 1-pinnate, while corresponding acroscopic pinnae are reduced to single pinnules. The stipe thus appears to branch dichotomously into 2 helically recurved rachises, with pinnate pinnae apparently arising from their upper sides, and each such pinnate pinna separated from its neighbours by a simple pinnule. Occasionally, a third lateral primary pinna undergoes helicoid branching, as illustrated in B.D. Duncan & G. Isaac, Ferns and Allied Plants of Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia: 140, fig. 13.9 (1986). The varieties recognised here represent extremes of a myriad of mutations and intergrades. A distinctive form confined to northern Cape York Peninsula has been included in var. hispidulum, although it probably warrants varietal status. C.J. Goudey, Maidenhair Ferns in Cultivation: 316--317 (1985), provides a description and photographs of the Cape York taxon. Infraspecific rank not recognised in all states.

Native to northern tropical Australia, mostly in eastern Queensland, but with some records from Christmas Island, Western Australia and the Northern Territory; sparingly naturalised in New South Wales. Occurs from Sri Lanka, throughout Indomalesia to subtropical China and New Caledonia; widely cultivated in tropical countries and, under glass, in temperate ones.

The species comprises a number of apparently distinctive entities, one of which, probably domesticated in China, has been long and widely cultivated including in Australia, where it is locally naturalised (e.g. Queensland, Chelona Shoal, Mackay, G.N. Batianoff 9303478, BRI); this is the Orange Jasmine, ‘Murraya exotica’, a form with rather small leathery leaflets: it is the Shan Fan or China Box (Needham 1986) used as a pesticide in Medieval China, especially to protect books from insects, though its status is still unclear and it may even represent a distinct wild species. Wild plants in Australia, with very few intermediate exceptions, from ‘dry’ semi-deciduous to deciduous vine thickets tend to be low sprawling shrubs less than 3 m high with small leaflets, highly aromatic when crushed, and pedicels 3--7 mm long; they are found from Cape York to southeast Queensland and there are some records from Western Australia and Northern Territory (‘Small Leaves’ of Brophy et al. (1994); see Mabberley (1998) for discussion). Plants from ‘less dry’ semi-deciduous notophyll forests form small trees 3--6 m high with larger leaflets, less aromatic when crushed, and pedicels 10--13 mm long; these have been recorded across northern tropical Australia (‘Big Leaves’ of Brophy et al. (1994)). Their relationship to plants in neighbouring territories is not yet fully elucidated. Recent work (Nguyen 2012), to be extended in scope, so far indicates that in using characters of leaflet shape and pubescence, besides molecular markers, i) the cultivated ‘M. exotica’ probably native only in southern China and northern Vietnam, is indeed argued to be specifically distinct from M. paniculata s. str. (native to Malesia), ii) the native Australian populations (also in Timor) of M. paniculata s. lat., are argued to be worthy of specific rank as ‘M. ovatifoliolata’, though that may not be the earliest available specific epithet. In general terms these taxa, at whatever rank, would therefore appear to be allopatric; however, according to Nguyen (2012), there are populations of putative hybrids (‘M. ×omphalocarpa Hayata’) between ‘M. exotica’ and ‘M. ovatifoliolata’ recorded from Lan Yu (off southern Taiwan), and also from western New Guinea, in neither of which localities have either of the suggested parental taxa so far been recorded. Murraya paniculata has been hybridised with species of Citrus, one of which also has pinnate leaves (Kubitzki et al. 2011) and at least one of which can be grafted on it (Swingle 1943). It is held to be a mosquito-repellent and a water-soluble toxin extracted from the leaves has been shown to kill eggs and nymphs of the Asian citrus blackfly. A treatment for Murraya paniculata occurring on Christmas Island is provided by Du Puy in Du Puy & Telford (1993: 303--304).

As treated here, includes forms often referred to as S. asperula N.A.Wakef. and S. dichotoma sensu Jones & Clemesha (1981) and Andrews (1990). Schizaea bifida and S. asperula are distinguished largely by the presence or absence of sterile fronds and the degree of sporogenous frond dichotomy. The former has sporogenous fronds unbranched or branched once or rarely twice; sterile fronds are rarely produced and, if present, are usually undivided. Schizaea asperula has sporogenous fronds branched several times, with sterile fronds shorter and more branched than sporogenous ones. In northern N.S.W. and south-eastern Qld a very robust Schizaea occurs which is often misidentified as S. dichotoma (see references above). This taxon resembles the more southerly S. asperula except that both sporogenous and sterile fronds are more divided. The smallest forms are found on wet, peaty soils in dwarf shrub-herbfields in alpine areas of Tas. where conditions are extreme and growing periods short. Two of the more recent sites supporting the species are very similar. Both are broad flats with impeded drainage, effectively permanently slightly inundated due to the high regional annual rainfall, and are surrounded by denser shrubby eucalypt woodland dominated by Eucalyptus nebulosa. Plants grow on the margins of the open sediment pans and on the edges of small slightly raised islands of heathy vegetation amongst the pans. Associated plant species include Leptospermum lanigerum, Baeckea leptocaulis, Sprengelia propinqua, Epacris glabella, Bauera rubioides and Gahnia grandis. The third site is on the gentle slope of the ridge above one of the other sites. Here plants are growing in better drained soils, but are still in small openings in otherwise denser vegetation. Elevation varies from c. 110--120 m (sites on flats) to c. 190 m (ridge site). All sites occur on Cambrian ultramafic geology, identified on geology maps as “dominantly serpentinised layered dunite and harzburgite”. The disturbance history of the area supporting the species is undocumented but includes some mineral extraction. Both the open sediment pan sites are on or close to old tracks and at least one appears to have been “worked over” (evidence of old mullock piles and that some of the drainage channels are the result of anthropogenic channelling). The openness of the sites is probably maintained by a combination of naturally poor drainage and fire events.

Known from one historical (probably 1870s) collection of unknown provenance (simply labelled “Tasmania”) and three more recent (2011--2012) collections. The latter collections are from one general area in the catchments of the Wilson and Harman Rivers, in the broader Pieman River watershed, west of Tullah, in the State’s central west; one site is c. 1 km from the others, separated from them by a major river, while the other two sites are c. 500 m apart, separated by dense shrubby vegetation seemingly highly unsuitable for the species.

The species was collected at some time in the 1800s, being represented in the Mueller Herbarium of the National Herbarium of Victoria (MEL). The undated fragmentary collection Scott MEL 4179 from an unknown locality in Tasmania, was noted under sect. Striatae by Barker (1982: 107) as being remarkable for its unusually proportionate leaf apex, and a narrowly attenuate leaf base not seen in glandular-hairy species of the section, being more akin to E. striata. “Scott” was most likely James Reid Scott (1839--1877), who arrived in Tasmania in 1856, and was a politician, surveyor, explorer and keen botanist. Between 1873 and 1876 he made various expeditions to little-explored parts of the west and southwest of Tasmania, reporting to the Minister of Lands that the area should be opened up and made accessible to encourage prospecting and mining (Smith 1976, Baillie 2010). The fact that Scott was interested in areas suitable for mining, supports the presumption that he may have collected his specimen from an area of high mineral prospectivity, such as ultramafic geology, which expresses itself obviously in the landscape and vegetation.

Little is known of the ecology of Euphrasia arguta. The discovered Nundle State Forest populations occupy open understorey of eucalypt forest with a mixed grass and shrub understorey, in sites that had been disturbed by logging or historic clearing. Historic records from Bathurst were in wet places in open forest and grassy country. It has been estimated as favouring grassy areas near rivers at elevations up to 700 m above sea level, with an annual rainfall of 600 mm (Benson & McDougall 2001: 332).
Recorded from New South Wales between Bathurst and the Patersons and Hunter Rivers to the south, and Walcha in the northeast. However, it is known now only from near Nundle.

The wide-ranging altitudinal and geographical distribution of Euphrasia collina is clearly the result of its ability to inhabit a correspondingly wide range of habitats. The various subspecies have more limited ecological preferences, their range of distribution often reflecting that of their habitats. Details are found in the notes on ecology under the treatments of the various subspecies. Evidence of the strong ecological limits on the ranges of distribution of the subspecies of Euphrasia collina is seen when two or more occur in the same region. Such instances of sympatry are described under E. collina: Intraspecific Polymorphism in Barker (1982: 163--173). In addition to ecological differences between the subspecies, there are some subspecies which are wider in their ecological requirements than others. These tend to have associated, often apparently clinal variation which can sometimes be related to an environmental gradation between the habitats or regions occupied by the morphological extremes.

The most common and widespread species of Euphrasia in Australia, being distributed throughout the temperate regions of the continent from sea level to the top of the highest summit, Mount Kosciuszko at 2230 m alt. Its 14 subspecies and several other variants, possibly warranting taxonomic recognition, have much more limited ranges of distribution. Details are included under the respective treatments.

By their possession of a single erect stem some first year plants of subsp. speciosa and subsp. paludosa may be confused with the annuals of sect. Scabrae. The perennials can easily be distinguished by the absence of branches from all but the lowest nodes. The annual species have branching in a more or less rigid basipetal sequence starting from a position one to a few nodes below the inflorescence and occurring in all lower nodes.

Widespread throughout lowland eastern Tasmania, in the southern lowland regions, the western highlands and (see note 1) possibly the southwestern edge of the eastern highlands of Victoria, and in the southeast corners of South Australia and New South Wales; near sea level to 750 m alt.

1. Subsp. collina and subsp. paludosa both occur in the western part of the eastern highlands of Victoria. Elsewhere in central and western Victoria, the two subspecies seem to occupy different areas of distribution, with subsp. collina mainly occurring in the western highlands and coastal regions, and subsp. paludosa being confined to the region of the basalt plains between Warrnambool and Port Phillip and to a possibly isolated occurrence in the region of Maryborough. However, many collections from outside the Grampians (Barker 1982: 149, fig. 50) are only tentatively placed in subsp. collina despite their uppermost leaves possessing a single pair of teeth typical of the subspecies. They contain only one or two plants and some could be uncommon variants from populations of subsp. paludosa. 2. Within subsp. collina there is geographical variation in the shape of the uppermost leaves of the stem or main inflorescence-bearing branches. The graph in Barker (1982: 180, fig. 64) portrays the variation in the length of the apical and marginal teeth of the uppermost leaves in different geographical areas throughout the range of the subspecies. The leaf type with longer, more acute teeth (Barker 1982: 18, fig. 6: Barker 1439, 1443, 1446) occurs in populations in the Grampians and nearby mountain areas. "E. collinoides" of Du Rietz (1948) probably belongs with these (see E. collina: note 4 in Barker 1982: 163). Leaves tending to the other type from southeast Tasmania with shorter, blunter teeth (Barker 1982: 18, fig. 6: Barker 953, 955, 968) are found along the Victorian coast extending eastwards from Anglesea into southern New South Wales. However, the whole range of variation in leaf shape is found in collections from the western plains of Victoria from the coast to north of the Grampians and in specimens from the western highlands (excluding the Grampians) and southern and western margins of the eastern highlands. Although the extreme types are apparently scattered throughout this area, within those collections containing several plants there is little variation. This variation in leaf shape is correlated with differences in the pattern of the sessile gland patches on the leaf undersurface (Barker 1982: 25).

In the alpine zone subsp. diemenica occupies open to rather dense heathland in flat areas or within screes. In the subalpine zone, where it is most commonly recorded, it occurs in grassland, dense to open areas of heath (Barker 1982: 184, fig. 66) or (Carolin 1222) "margins of beech forest". There is one record (Barker 1141) from wet sclerophyll forest "in burnt area among regenerating Eucalyptus". The allied lowland to montane variant (note 2 in Barker 1982: 187) has been recorded from grassy areas associated with Eucalyptus wet to dry sclerophyll forest (Barker 923) and wet soil at edge of a Baumea swamp (Harwood 110). The Mount Brown, Tasman Peninsula, population occurs on an exposed dolerite slab in crevices with other herbs and scattered shrubs.

Endemic to Tasmania, where it is restricted to the subalpine and alpine zones of the isolated north-east mountains, the Central Plateau, the south-central mountain systems of Mount Field and Mount Wellington, and the Cradle Mountain-Hampshire Hills region which forms the northernmost extension of the Western Mountains. There is one collection from the mid-west of the island from Mount King William (F.A. Rodway NSW 22287) at the southern end of the Western Mountains; another comes from Port Davey in the extreme south-west (F.H. Long s.n. HO 22109) which is somewhat atypical of the subspecies (note 3 in Barker 1982: 188). Flowering occurs mainly between December and mid-February, although flowering specimens have been collected as early as the beginning of September (Stead NSW 64341) and as late as the end of March (Wimbush NSWNP). Mature fruits are evident at the start of January.

In the alpine zone subsp. diversicolor is especially common in tall alpine herbfield (Barker 1982: 226, fig. 77), but it sometimes occurs in heath and (Costin et al. 1979) drier sites of sod tussock grassland. In subalpine regions the subspecies is less common and generally grows on the margins of sphagnum bogs. It avoids sod tussock grassland, a principal habitat of subsp. paludosa. However, at Spencers Creek crossing on the Kosciuszko summit road it was found not only on bog margins, but also in a community apparently similar to tall alpine herbfield. Similarly, on Long Plain, north of Kiandra, a lone population (Barker 1663) is confined to a small area of herbfield within extensive sod tussock grassland (note 4 in Barker 1982: 228).

Endemic to the alpine and subalpine zones of the Snowy Mountains of south-eastern New South Wales; 1370--2230 m alt. It is apparently absent from the subalpine zone on the summit of the Brindabella Range even though it occurs on the lower-lying northward extension of the subalpine grasslands of the Snowy Mountains which reach the base of these mountains (note 4 in Barker 1982: 228). The Gibbo-Pinnibar-Pilot-Cobberas mountain system is poorly botanised. Its presence there should be investigated, though there is a closely-related but divergent form on the Cobberas (note 2 in Barker 1982: 227).

I. Subsp. diversicolor is sympatric with subsp. glacialis, subsp. lapidosa and subsp. paludosa in parts of its range. It retains its morphological and ecological differences, except where there is ecotonal intergradation into subsp. glacialis and in a single known instance of hybridisation with subsp. paludosa (see E. collina: Intraspecific Polymorphism in Barker 1982). 2. Populations from tall alpine herbfields in the Kosciuszko area and the higher mountains to the north are characterised by large, broad leaves, often broadest near the base and often with bluntish-tipped apical and marginal teeth (Barker 1982: 21, fig. 9: Barker 1684, 1703, 1704), long calyces and long corollas with long broad lower lips (Barker 1982: 226, fig. 77C). Plants found growing in sphagnum bogs (Barker 1982: 228, fig. 78) in the upper parts of the subalpine zone about Kosciuszko have smaller leaves with typical teeth but with less truncate bases (Barker 1982: 21, fig. 9: Barker 1701) and flowers which tend to be smaller with narrower lovver corollas lobes (Barker 1982: 228, fig. 78B). The plants often set less fruit, and the roots and lower branches, which are encased in sphagnum, are very slender. Such bogs occur at Spencers Creek near the Mt Kosciuszko road. The plants growing in the bog area but not within the sphagnum itself (Barker 1982: 21, fig. 9: Barker 1702) have uppermost leaves more similar to those of plants within the sphagnum (Barker 1982: 21, fig. 9: Barker 1710) than those of plants within the nearby herbfield (Barker 1982: 21, fig. 9: Barker 1703). However their root system and leafy lower parts of branches resemble the latter. In the watersheds of the lower altitudes to the north where tussock grasslands mainly replace the herbfields of the higher regions, plants of subsp. diversicolor are usually associated with sphagnum bogs, although they do not grow within the sphagnum. These plants (e.g. Barker 1982: 21, fig. 9: Barker 1677) tend to be intermediate between the sphagnum and herbfield forms of the Kosciuszko region in leaf and floral characters.

There are insufficient ecological data on herbarium labels to gain a picture of the range of habitats which have been occupied by subsp. muelleri. Those available (Stirling 166, Mueller MEL 41378) indicate an open meadow habitat. The annotations on two mixed herbarium sheets, possibly also pertaining to subsp. muelleri, refer to damp places (Mueller MEL 41379, Anon. MEL 41410).

Old collections of Euphrasia collina subsp. muelleri indicate that the subspecies was once widely distributed on the mainland of Australia from northern New South Wales near the Queensland border throughout mainland south-eastern Australia, and westwards as far as the Mount Lofty and Southern Flinders Ranges of South Australia. There are many more collections from central and western Victoria than from New South Wales and South Australia, which, from the many collections made of Euphrasia in the respective areas in the 19th century, indicates the subspecies was rare outside these parts of Victoria. In 1982 when the genus was revised by Barker (1982) only two collections had been made since 1907; they came from Frankston, the Melbourne suburb on the western side of Port Phillip Bay, in 1947 and 1949. Altitudinal data are lacking; it occupied lowland and at least low mountain habitats.

A few collections diverge in the indumentum of the calyces, bracts and upper leaves from typical subsp. muelleri (fig. 53, Barker 182: 150). Several collections from western Victoria and south-eastern New South Wales (Mueller GH p.p., Crouch MEL 41431, Eckert 29, Reader 9, Coveny & Rodd 886, Sullivan 43, Whan NSW 10940) bear sparse to dense glandular hairs 0.05--0.1mm long, mixed with the moderately densely to densely eglandular scabrous or scaberulous indumentum characteristic of subsp. muelleri. Still other forms apparently confined to the Southern and Central Tablelands and South-western Slopes regions of New South Wales, and possibly in Victoria near the Snowy Mountains, bear woolly eglandular hairs 0.2--0.5 mm long on the upper parts, with the indumentum shorter lower down (Bull MEL 41486, Rawes 34, Curran MEL 41719). There are two similar specimens (mounted with a densely glandular plant related to subsp. speciosa) in Anon MEL 41503 from nearby in New South Wales; they bear dense woolly eglandular hairs c. 0.2 mm long mixed with very short glandular hairs on the bracts and rachis, and also differ from typical subsp. muelleri by their very elongated inflorescences with long pedicels and long narrow leaves with 1 or 2 pairs of teeth. The long-woolly eglandular variants lacking glandular hairs may be extremes of variation in normal populations of subsp. muelleri; Mueller MEL 41375 and French MEL 41748 contain some plants with the scabrous indumentum typical of the subspecies, and others with a longer, more lax indumentum in the upper parts. However, the glandular variants of subsp. muelleri are more likely to represent one or two distinct taxa or intergrades with subsp. speciosa. To establish the true relationships between subsp. muelleri and these variants surviving populations of each must be found.

Occupies a wide range of habitats. In the subalpine zone of south eastern Australia it is common in sparse to dense snowgum (Eucalyptus pauciflora) woodland and sod-tussock grassland, but sometimes also occurs in heath or areas of shrubs in sparse snowgum woodland, or in grassy areas associated with bogs or swamps. On the summit of Mount Speculation, Victoria, it occurs above the tree-line in a herbfield with scattered shrubs (Barker 1543). In lower mountain regions of south-eastern Australia it is common in wet or dry sclerophyll forest or grassy clearings between, but has also been recorded in association with swamps or in "damp heath". In western coastal regions there are records from heath and swampy sites. Finally, there is one record (Anon. 44) from a sand hill apparently near Walmer in the southwestern plains of New South Wales. There are no data concerning the South Australian localities. The subspecies has been recorded in sandy to clay soils associated commonly with granite, but also with shale, sandstone or sedimentary rocks.

Widely spread in eastern Australia from the Mount Lofty Ranges of South Australia, an old record, to the very south of Queensland. The subspecies is most common in the montane and subalpine regions of eastern Victoria and New South Wales. In southern Queensland it is known from only two old collections. In South Australia the subspecies was confined to the Mount Lofty Ranges, which is a noted refuge area for plant species common in the wetter climates of southeastern Australia and apparently more widespread in previous cooler and wetter times (e.g. Parsons 1973); it is now apparently extinct. Subsp. paludosa also occurs in the regions of Victoria between Port Phillip and Warrnambool and probably near Maryborough (note 1), and in the coastal regions of New South Wales, north of Botany Bay. Altitude, near sea level to 1900 m.

In subsp. paludosa there are variations in characters of indumentum and seed size which are apparently related to altitude and geographical distribution. Subsessile glandular hairs (see Barker 1982: 13) are confined to populations at higher altitudes particularly in the Snowy Mountains of New South Wales, and are especially dense on plants of the higher parts of the Mt Kosciusko region near Charlottes Pass (e.g. Barker 1700, Johnson & Constable NSW15760). They are much sparser or sometimes completely absent on plants of lower subalpine areas, both in the Mt Kosciusko region and in the extensive tussock grass-lands to the north. Occurrences of these hairs outside the Snowy Mountains seem limited to two localities. Specimens in the subalpine woodland of theBrindabella Range (e.g. Barker 1644) bear subsessile glandular hairs mainly on the calyx; in other subalpine or montane sites only non-glandular plants seem to occur. In the summit populations of Mt Speculation, Victoria (Barker 1542--1543), rare plants have subsessile glandular hairs mainly confined to the lower leaves, but the majority lack these glands. Seeds are generally larger in ssp. paludosa in the Kosciusko region (usually 1.0--1.4 mm long), where plants invariably bear a sparse to dense indumentum of subsessile glandular hairs. This, however, seems to be an independent altitudinal phenomenon as elsewhere populations with subsessile glandular hairs have the more normal smaller seeds (usually 0.6--1.1mm long). Similar reduction in seed size with lower altitude is seen in other taxa and groups of taxa in the genus in Australia (p. 35). Because of the large number of populations with only a partial incidence of the scattered subsessile glandular hairs and the lack of a strong correlation of their presence with other character differences, formal taxonomic recognition is unwarranted. 3. In subsp. paludosa branching is restricted to the regions of the axes at or near ground level throughout most subalpine and montane areas. However, specimens with branches or shoots occurring well up the main axes are rather common in the montane regions of northern New South Wales and southern Queensland. This type of habit also predominates in the collections from the coastal areas of New South Wales north of Newcastle, Mt Stanley (Canning 364) and Mt Granya (Walter MEL41306) which are isolated mountains of north-eastern Victoria, East Gippsland (Sayer MEL41323, MEL41324), and the Dandenong Ranges and other more westerly montane and lowland areas on the edge of the eastern highlands of Victoria (Gargurevich MEL41373, Walter NSW10944, A K30649).

Commonly occupies sandy soil, in the mallee-heaths of the inland plains of south-eastern South Australia and western Victoria, in heathland of coastal cliff-tops with underlying limestone on southern Yorke Peninsula, Kangaroo Island and possibly south-western Western Australia, and on coastal dunes and the swales between across southern Australia. The unusual population on West Cape, southern Yorke Peninsula, grows in very limited soil in cracks in the exposed limestone cliff-top (Barker 1982: note 3: 195, fig. 70). Atypical records of habitat are "Lateritic soils. Eucalyptus cladocalyx dominant" (D. Smith 309A) and "Granite rock" (Lullfitz 3558).

Restricted mainly to the coastal regions of south-western Western Australia and South Australia with an inland extension into the sandy-mallee heaths of the 90-Mile Desert in South Australia and the Little Desert and Big Desert of western Victoria. A few old collections come from Tasmania, the only specific localities being at Woolnorth and Circular Head (or Stanley) on the north-west coast. In South Australia, there are three isolated, possibly relict occurrences at Mount Kitchener in the Mount Lofty Ranges, Mount Remarkable in the southern Flinders Ranges and in the Gawler Ranges (Barker 1982: 149, fig. 51: note 4). Altitude, sea level to c. 150 m; there are no records for the isolated inland populations in South Australia.

1. Within subsp. tetragona there is geographical variation in leaf shape and the extent of branching into the upper parts of the stem and main inflorescence-bearing branches. This variation is illustrated in a graph in Barker (1982: 193, fig. 69) of the length: breadth ratio of the upper leaves of the main axes plotted against the proportion simple of the height of the inflorescence on the main axis above ground level. It should be noted that the selection of specimens in some cases is neither complete nor random, but has been based on an attempt to obtain the whole range of variation. The Kangaroo Island populations are represented by all entire plants in the available herbarium material. In addition, although incomplete, the only plants from the northern side of the island (Ashby 1400) are included, as they appear to relate more to the mainland populations than those from the southern coast of the island. Except for the inland collections, which are apparently relict (see note 4), a very *atypical collection (Eichler 14044) from Corny Point, and the collection Mueller MEL 41408 from the extreme east of the mainland occurrences of subsp. tetragona (but see note 1), the south coast Kangaroo Island populations differ from the mainland populations by their extremely high aerial branching on the main inflorescence bearing axes. They also have a tendency to have broader leaves than their counterparts on the neighbouring peninsulas, although the differences may not prove statistically significant (Barker 1982: 19, fig. 7: Eichler 15384, Barker 1355). However, it is clear that plants from the sandy mallee heaths of the 90-Mile Desert, the Little Desert and the Big Desert in the eastern part of the mainland range of distribution, diverge from populations to the west by their narrower upper leaves (Barker 1982: 19, fig. 7: Barker 1450). These leaves are very similar in shape and size to those found in subsp. collina in the adjacent areas of inland western Victoria (Barker 1982: 18, fig. 6: Barker 1439, 1443, 1446), and reflect the close taxonomic affinities of the two subspecies. 2. Growing on the extreme tip of West Cape, south-western Yorke Peninsula, occurs a population of subsp. tetragona (Barker 1374, Barker 1982: 195, fig. 70) unique in its large broad, very fleshy leaves (Barker 1982: 19, fig. 7), calyces and bracts, and short inflorescence-bearing branches. The plants grow with other succulent plants in very exposed conditions in sparse soil in crevices of the limestone which tops the promontory. Plants (Barker 1375) typical of coastal populations of southern Yorke Peninsula occur behind the headland in the more protected slopes of sand dunes. The increased fleshiness in the cliff-top plants is probably because of the greater exposure to sea-spray, a response often exhibited by plants in such areas (e.g. Specht 1972). Plants on less-exposed cliffs such as those near Corny Point are typical of the subspecies. Whether there is any genetic basis to these differences is not known. 3. In South Australia subsp. tetragona is recorded well to the north of its common range of distribution (Barker 1982: 149, fig. 51) in three widely disjunct mountain areas, the Gawler Ranges (Sullivan MEL 41413 and a possible duplicate Anon. MEL 41752), Mount Remarkable in the southern Flinders Ranges (Mueller HBG, p.p.), and Kaiserstuhl (now Mount Kitchener) in the Barossa Range (Mueller MEL 41488 and possibly Mueller MEL 41513, which is so similar it may be a duplicate). Despite the individual records probably being based on single old collections, the coincidence of three such isolated locations in the same general region points to their authenticity. The three mountain ranges have been proposed as part of a series of refugia for plants formerly occupying lowlands between in wetter climatic periods (Crocker & Wood 1947, Boomsma 1972, Parsons 1973, Kraehenbuehl unpubl.). This pattern of distribution in subsp. tetragona would seem to be unusual, as it involves a predominantly sandy mallee-heath plant apparently with isolated occurrences in what are basically refuges for montane sclerophyll forest or woodland taxa.

Occurs in dense local populations from the subalpine zone to the tops of the highest summits. It has been recorded from subalpine Snowgum (Eucalyptus pauciflora) woodland, where it favours the more open areas, from alpine heath, especially in areas of low shrubs, although it is sometimes found in tall dense shrubberies, and from tall alpine herbfield. It appears to be absent from the subalpine tussock grassland in the Mount Cope-Pretty Valley area of the Bogong High Plains.

Confined to two neighbouring mountain areas in the Victorian Alps; all 3 subspecies endemic to Victoria. It is most diverse in the region bound on the south by the extensive Bogong High Plains and the higher regions of the Dargo High Plains, on the north-east by Mount Bogong, which is the highest mountain in Victoria, and on the west by the Mount Feathertop-Mount Hotham-The Twins ridge. It also occurs on the isolated granitic Mount Buffalo plateau which is north-west of the "main divide" of the Alps; 1200--2000 m alt.

Intraspecific polymorphism The pure populations of the taxa Three subspecies are recognised under Euphrasia crassiuscula. Their altitudinal occurrence and areas of distribution (are different, but overlapping. Figure 81 in Barker (1982: 239) portrays the known distribution of the three taxa concerned and their intermediates. In addition it shows the variation in the diagnostically important characters of anther pilosity, corolla colour, and indumentum in often extensive population samples covering much of the range of the species. The distribution and altitudinal range of pure populations of subsp. glandulifera are very similar to subsp. eglandulosa, although populations of the former are much rarer than those of either of the other subspecies. In contrast to the other two subspecies, subsp. crassiuscula occupies a lower altitudinal range and its range of distribution hardly overlaps with them. There is little apparent difference in the ecological preferences of subsp. eglandulosa and subsp. crassiuscula. Both occur in alpine heath and subalpine woodland. Subsp. glandulifera, however, has not been recorded from snowgum woodland communities. A geographical variation pattern in the density of the woolly marginal indumentum of the leaves, bracts and calyces seems evident. All populations of both subsp. crassiuscula (Barker 1601) and subsp. glandulifera which occur in the Bogong High Plains area exhibit a denser indumentum than their populations to the west. These latter plants have a density similar to that of subsp. eglandulosa throughout its range. The taxonomic and phylogenetic significance of this is unclear. Intergradation between the taxa The two similarly distributed taxa, subsp. eglandulosa and subsp. glandulifera, apparently remain completely distinct from each other. On Mount Nelse (Barker 1595, 1596; Willis MEL 41551, MEL 41555) and Mount Feathertop (Barker 1573, 1574) they are found as easily distinguishable populations with no detectable intergradation. Populations intermediate between each of these taxa respectively and the generally allopatric subsp. crassiuscula occur in the Feathertop-Hotham area. Except for possibly one case on Mount Loch (see below), populations of the two eastern taxa apparently never occur beside populations of subsp. crassiuscula without morphological intergradation. Subsp. crassiuscula and subsp. glandulifera intergrade in alpine and subalpine localities on The Razorback between Mounts Hotham and Feathertop (Barker 1579) and on the slopes of Mount Feathertop itself (Barker 1575). It is unclear whether the two subspecies remain as distinct populations or are intermixed near the summit of Mount Loch (Barker 1561, Briggs NSW 126383). The differences between subsp. eglandulosa and subsp. crassiuscula break down to some extent on the rounded summit area of Mount Hotham (Barker 1551, 1553, 1554) and on the saddle between Mount Hotham and Mount Loch (Barker 1563). Two variants occur on Mount Hotham (Barker 1974). The populations apparently allied to subsp. eglandulosa by their white, frequently extensively striated corollas, encompass the variation in anther back indumentum typical of both subspecies (Barker 1982: 239, fig. 81). In contrast, subsp. crassiuscula retains its integrity, even in a situation where populations of both variants overlap while flowering simultaneously. The extensive grazing and erosion that have occurred over the past century in these areas (Costin 1957, 1962; Carr & Turner 1959) should be considered as a cause of breakdown of ecogenetic barriers in any further study of how these races evolved.

Occurs in a wide range of habitats. From specimen annotations it appears most frequent in open grassy situations, possibly ones which are wet. However, it is perhaps less common in permanently wet sites than the closely allied Euphrasia caudata, E. ciliolata and, possibly, E. orthocheila. It has also been recorded from sand associated with dunes and salt lakes along the coasts of South and Western Australia, and in dry heath and dry forest land in south-eastern Australia and Tasmania.

Occurs throughout most of temperate, non-arid Australia and Tasmania, reaching as far north as Sydney on the east coast, and extending into the south-west of Western Australia. It ranges in altitude from sea level up to 1100 m in Tasmania and to about 1500 m on the Australian mainland, including some subalpine or high montane sites (see Intraspecific Polymorphism in Notes).

Intraspecific polymorphism In the Australian Alps between the Mount Kosciuszko region and the Bogong High Plains there is a breakdown of a number of the many morphological differences between Euphrasia scabra of lowland and lower montane sites and E. caudata. Studies are showing that new species are involved, and further, that more than one species is evident in lowland mainland Australia.

A widespread species showing considerable variation, sometimes geographically correlated, but for the most part not sufficiently discontinuous to allow reliable recognition of infraspecific taxa. Some specimens from the Shark Bay area and along the coast almost to Carnarvon have been separated as Anthocercis sp. Shark Bay (T.E.H. Aplin 3335) (Western Australian Herbarium 1998-). They have a more openly branched inflorescence, similar to that found in A. ilicifolia, but quite slender, pale yellow flowers, more characteristic of some forms of A. littorea. They are included here for the time being but are under investigation with a view to their possible recognition as a separate taxon at species or infraspecific level. Like many related species, A. littorea is known to contain alkaloids of some toxicity but records of poisoning of stock and humans (children) (Gardner & Bennetts 1956, Cannon et al. 1969) are unsubstantiated and of uncertain identity - they may be based on material now known to represent the separate species A. ilicifolia. The fruit of A. littorea are often malformed due to galling (e.g. see Scott & Negus 2002: 173, fig. 2). It can be difficult to distinguish between A. littorea and A. ilicifolia, and they are sometimes misidentified in the literature (see notes in Illustration citations below). In the account of A. littorea by Dixon (2011: 86--87), the flowers depicted for the species appear to actually be A. ilicifolia subsp. ilicifolia, and the capsule is consistent for that taxon. Cultivated tomatoes also usually have 6--9-lobed corollas and/or calyces (rather than 5-lobed), multilocular ovaries (rather than 2-locular) and tend to have larger leaves. Feral forms will revert to the small fruited wild type morphology. Ordinarily the species bears only 5-merous flowers with bilocular ovaries. However, the two species are readily separated on leaf size and shape (where the two species occur together), distribution of leaf stomata and ﬂower sexuality. No apparent hybrids were encountered during ﬁeld studies or in herbarium material. The variant that has been referred to as Hymenanthera sp. aff. dentata (East Gippsland variant) Vic. Herbarium (CHAH, http://www.anbg.gov.au/chah/apc/about-APC.html) (= Melicytus sp. aff. dentatus (East Gippsland variant) sensu Ross and Walsh (2003)) is, we believe, merely a shade form that may be encountered throughout the range of the species. The leaf dimensions are indicated by the bracketed upper dimensions in the description above. A specimen of this form at Kew herbarium from the Brodribb River in eastern Victoria was labelled H. banksii var. latifolia by Mueller (K 000370100). This name was never published. Although throughout its range, most populations of Melicytus dentatus are dioecious, six collections of apparently hermaphroditic plants from New South Wales were encountered among herbarium material. These were from Rylstone (R.T. Baker s.n., NSW 641357 and R.T. Baker s.n, 641360), near StuartTown (R.O. Makinson 1201, MEL, NE, NSW), Sydney area (Penrith, B.M. Wiecek 6789, MEL, NSW), Warrumbungle National Park (The Canyon, W. Greuter 20675, NSW) and Wollemi National Park (Widdin Brook, R. Story 6772, CANB, NSW). Fieldwork is required to determine whether the entire populations are hermaphroditic or whether the specimens represent occasional plants among predominantly dioecious populations. One of two plants grown at Lincoln (New Zealand) from seed collected from a female plant at Canberra was hermaphroditic (B.P.J. Molloy, pers. obs.), suggesting that occasional hermaphroditic plants may indeed occur within populations of ‘normal’ dioecious plants. The frequency of this appears to be so low that the species may be described as essentially dioecious. The existence of hermaphroditic ﬂowers in the two collections from New South Wales populations may also suggest the possibility of either gynodioecy or cosexuality within these populations, or both.

Tribulopis angustifolia shows considerable variation in hair covering, flower size, ornamentation of the cocci, length of the style, size of the fruit and the number of spines on the fruit. Specimens with both medial and basal spines on the fruitlets are usually to be found in the more southerly part of the distribution. Specimens in which the fruits lack spines are usually larger-flowered and apparently short-lived perennials (because of the possession of a tap root); they are more likely to be associated with beach localities or deep sands of the N coast and in the areas N of Katherine. Collections from the Mt Isa region, segregated as T. aff. angustifolia (Mt Isa) in Barker (1998) are distinctive by the appressed rather than erect hairs on the ovary, their wider leaflets (2--3.5 mm wide) and their shorter styles (1.5--1.8 mm long); however the species is so variable they have not been segregated here.

Despite being the subject of a number of searches for biological control agents elsewhere, it is difficult to look at introducing many of these agents to Australia because of the presence of native Tribulus species. A review of the agents considered for Australia can be found in Scott (1990, 2012). Many claims are made for the use of T. terrestris supplements in increasing testosterone levels and for, amongst other claims, body building purposes. Such supplements are certainly readily available but there are variable claims as to their efficacy. The whole plant has a long history of medicinal use in India and China. In N.S.W., grazing of T. terrestris causes “staggers” in sheep (Bourke et al., 1992), nitrate poisoning in sheep and cattle and is also associated with photosensitisation (Weed Management Unit (2009). Tribulus terrestris s. lat. consists of a number of taxa which overlap in distribution and imperceptibly intergrade in morphology. Three of these taxa have already been recognised at species level within Australia (T. terrestris, T. micrococcus and T. minutus) and it is not proposed to change the classification here, even though it can be difficult to apply and there has to be some doubt concerning the validity of the species recognised. Tribulus terrestris has been further subdivided in the past to recognise two forms of differing style length which have an approximate northern and southern Australia distribution, but these have not been formally recognised here. The group is very much in need of revision both within Australia and world-wide. It is a very good candidate for molecular study if we wish to understand relationships between the taxa in Australia and their overseas counterparts; the forms encountered presumably represent introductions of different forms of the species since T. terrestris is also very variable outside Australia, but there may well be new forms appearing with hybridisation with Australian species. Chromosome studies by Morrison & Scott (1996) have already revealed variable ploidy levels both in Australia and overseas and they also point to a number of introductions to Australia. Germination of some seed any time after a rain event, dying back to an extensive root system in dry conditions and the ability to produce, in a very short time (6 weeks according to a number of sources), numerous fruit which are very effectively distributed by the activities of man, means that these plants are formidable weeds which are extremely difficult to combat. A number of insect visitors have been documented as effecting cross-pollination, while self-pollination occurs should there be no visitations, resulting in the potential for 100% seed set (Reddi et al. 1981). Estimates of the number of fruits per plant range from 200 to 5000, with each of these fruits usually having 5 cocci containing 2--5 seeds. The two main diverging spines, combined with shorter spines, all at differing angles, facilitate attachment and hence dispersal by animals or vehicles. Contamination of crops and wool is a problem for the agricultural industry.
